source_refs.note: X-linked Dominant Traits: a main subheading of 18.8.1 Sex-linked Traits in Humans, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 107-108.

blocks.text: Such traits are in equal ratio in females and males. Examples include vitamin D-resistant rickets (inability to properly metabolize vitamin D, leading to softening and weakening of bones), Rett syndrome (neuro-developmental disorder with loss of speech, repetitive hand movements, and problems with walking), Aicardi syndrome (abnormal development of brain).
book_errors: in equal ratio in females and males

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says X-linked dominant traits are in equal ratio in females and males. In fact they are more common in females, because a female has two X chromosomes and so two chances of carrying the allele; the book’s own next point, that an affected father passes the trait to all his daughters and to none of his sons, shows this.

blocks.alt: Person icons. A mother with the trait XRXr and a non-carrier father XrY. Eggs XR and Xr; sperm Xr and Y. Lines join them to four children: daughters XRXr (trait present) and XrXr (non-carrier); sons XRY (trait present) and XrY (non-carrier). Key: R, X-linked dominant allele; r, X-linked recessive allele.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.16: Inheritance of X-linked dominant traits (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.16).

blocks.text: If an X-linked dominant trait is present in mother (homozygous or heterozygous), 50% of her offspring can inherit the trait. If such trait is present in father, all of his daughters will inherit it (a daughter inherits her father’s X-chromosome) and no son will inherit it (a son does not inherit his father’s X-chromosome).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The 50% applies only to a heterozygous mother. A mother homozygous for an X-linked dominant allele gives it to every child, so all her offspring inherit the trait.
